" *

* Converts the given Java version string to an int. *

* *

* Example return values: *

*
    *
  • 120 for Java 1.2
    • *
  • 131 for Java 1.3.1
    • *
  • 160 for Java 1.6.0_20
    • *
* *

* Patch releases are not reported. *

*

* This method is package private instead of private to support unit test invocation. *

* * @return the version, for example 131 for Java 1.3.1 "

Title: Diagnosis
Details:
- Failing test: org.apache.commons.lang3.SystemUtilsTest.testJavaVersionAsInt() asserts that SystemUtils.toJavaVersionInt(null) returns 0.

- Implementation found:
  - org.apache.commons.lang3.SystemUtils.toJavaVersionInt(String) is declared as returning float:
    - It delegates to toVersionInt(toJavaVersionIntArray(version, JAVA_VERSION_TRIM_SIZE)).
  - org.apache.commons.lang3.SystemUtils.toJavaVersionIntArray(String, int) returns an int[]; for null input it returns ArrayUtils.EMPTY_INT_ARRAY.
  - org.apache.commons.lang3.SystemUtils.toVersionInt(int[]) returns an int and, for an empty array, returns 0.
  - JAVA_VERSION_TRIM_SIZE is 3.

- Javadoc for toJavaVersionInt(String) states it “Converts the given Java version string to an int” and gives examples like 120, 131, 160, confirming the intended return type is int.

- What happens at runtime:
  - For null input, toJavaVersionIntArray returns an empty int[].
  - toVersionInt on an empty array returns the int 0.
  - That int 0 is then implicitly widened to a float due to the mistaken method signature, so toJavaVersionInt(null) returns 0.0f.

- Why the assertion fails:
  - The test calls assertEquals(0, SystemUtils.toJavaVersionInt(null)).
  - Because the actual value is a float, Java chooses the Object-based overload via autoboxing (Integer vs Float) rather than an int-int overload. Integer.valueOf(0).equals(Float.valueOf(0.0f)) is false, causing the assertion to fail even though the numeric value is effectively 0.

- Root cause:
  - The return type of SystemUtils.toJavaVersionInt(String) is incorrectly declared as float instead of int, contradicting its name, Javadoc, and usage in tests. The core logic yields 0 for null as expected; only the wrong return type leads to the failure.

- Relation to the issue report:
  - The report mentions parsing/version handling issues (getJavaVersionAsFloat throwing StringIndexOutOfBoundsException on Android). While that speaks to broader version parsing concerns, the immediate test failure is due to a signature/type mismatch in toJavaVersionInt rather than an exception path. The inconsistency likely stems from refactoring or confusion with the float-returning API while working on version parsing.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
